text.text: WordStar 7, the last ever DOS version, is re-released for free
The preferred tool of Arthur C Clarke, Anne Rice and George R R Martin
Before WordPerfect, the most popular work processor was WordStar. Now, the last ever DOS version has been bundled and set free by one of its biggest fans.
Wordstar 7 on macOS - click to enlarge

texts.text: WordStar 7.0d was the last-ever DOS release of
classic word processor, and it still has admirers today. A
is Canadian SF writer Robert J Sawyer, who wrote the book that became the
TV series

Thanks to his efforts you can now try out this pinnacle of pre-Windows PC programs for professional prose-smiths. Sawyer has taken the final release, packaged it up along with some useful tools — including DOS emulators for modern Windows – and
. Now you, too, can revel in the sheer unbridled power of this powerful app.

text.text: The program has been a big part of my career – not only did I write all 25 of my novels and almost all of my short stories with it (a few date back to the typewriter era), I also in my earlier freelance days wrote hundreds of newspaper and magazine articles with WordStar.

texts.text: The download is 680MB, but as well as the app itself, full documentation, and some tools to help translate WordStar documents to more modern formats, it also includes copies of two FOSS tools that will let you run this MS-DOS application on modern Windows:
and
. Regular
readers may recognize both from our story on

text.text: how to run DOS on a 64-bit OS

texts.text: from last year. Sawyer also offers a
[PDF].
WordStar has a long and exceptionally involved history, as the Wordstar.org fan site
. It started out on CP/M, was ported to DOS, multiple incompatible programs of the same name launched, and later still
. The last ever release was part of an
. Sawyer is correct: the final DOS version really is the true classic.
MicroPro, the company behind WordStar, was repeatedly acquired. At one point it was part of SoftKey, which was acquired and became
, which was
in what
"the worst acquisition of all time." As a result, the software business was spun off again and bought by
. Sawyer says:

text.text: It was last updated in December 1992, and the company that made it has been defunct for decades; the program is abandonware.

texts.text: While it certainly has been abandoned since the end of the 20th century, the term "abandonware" isn't a legal one. It's not clear to us who owns the intellectual property. We doubt it's one of the surviving offshoots, today's
, but it could be another offshoot,
. Either way, it's very unlikely that the owners will care.
If the many changes of ownership weren't enough, the program itself had many offshoots. A rewrite in C became the incompatible

, that abandoned the keyboard-centric UI which was WordStar's hallmark. MicroPro also acquired a student's Modula-2 project and rebadged it WordStar Express, which Amstrad PC 1512 owners may remember: Amstrad got a licence cheaply and bundled it as "WordStar 1512". Even WordStar 7 isn't based on the original code: MicroPro bought a rival clone of the program called NewWord, and made it the official WordStar 4 – as still

text.text: used by George R R Martin

texts.text: While many folks in the Unix world have Vi keystrokes engraved in their muscle memory, those for WordStar are the equivalent for CP/M and MS-DOS users of a certain age.
for navigation,
to mark the start of a block,
to mark the end, then
to copy it or
to move it; and
to Save. The modern
still uses them, for instance. It hasn't got all the functionality, but if you don't want to struggle with an emulator to run a DOS app, the FOSS clone
comes close, and has

text.text: versions for Windows, Linux and macOS

texts.text: By modern standards, WordStar doesn't do much, but it does everything many writers want. The

FOSS desk is rather fond of Robert Sawyer's novels, as well as George R R Martin's come to that, but those less given to genre fiction may recognize William F Buckley Jr and Ralph Ellison, both keen users. ®

Estava comentando com o @fsanches como o assembly do TLCS tem bons mnemônicos para saltos condicionais. Aí na página dois a gente vê isso 👆
Só pra morder a língua.
A descrição dos mnemônicos de rotação é quase isso aqui.

Dá pra entender, mas é meio bizarro. As versões sem carry são uma rotação de 8 bits em que o bit que dá a volta é copiado para a flag carry, enquanto as versões com carry são uma rotação de 9 bits em que a flag carry atua como bit mais significante
O problema é a nomenclatura. Porque escolheram RLC pra significar SEM carry quando o fato de ter um "C" no mnemônico ali serviria justamente pra dizer que essa é a versão COM carry.
Ou indo pelo outro lado: se você vê o mnemônico RLC sem saber nada específico sobre assembly de TLCS, você imagina que significaria "Rotate Left com Carry". 😂
Mas é igual no Z80, não?
De fato, foi o Z80 quem começou esse crime hediondo.
E no Z80 temos RLC/RRC e RL/RR, mas SLA/SRA e SLL/SRL 🤷🏽‍♂

Para mim esse é o exemplo de tanto faz. Coloca o nome longo num define e boa.

Esse é o vídeo: 

https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tORBhP2e_ok
e nesse frame dá pra ver as 4 ROMs e as duas CPUs
Em outro frame dá pra ver o modelo da CPU: TOSHIBA TMP95C061AF (idêntica à do NeoGeoPocket)
Direfente, mas muito parecida, com as CPUs do KN5000 (que são TOSHIBA TMP94C241)

O pulo do gato aqui é o seguinte... Eu acho que eu  posso aprender mais sobre o protocolo de comunicação inter-CPUs do KN5000 vendo o disasm da CPU secundária do WSA1(R). Pois aposto que o protocolo é o mesmo. E apesar de eu não ter o dump da bootrom da subcpu do kn5000, no caso do WSA1(r) essas ROMs são soquetadas e alguém já fez o dump
olhando no video anotei o código das etiquetas e com isso achei numa busca no Google um site que hospeda dumps de ROMs de synths
então tenho aqui os dumps dessas 4 ROMs

Ah! e sabe por que são 4 ROMs?

Por que são duas CPUs de 32 bits de barramento de dados. Então cada uma delas usa um par de ROMs 27C4002, que têm 16 bits de dados.
Comprei o service manual do WSA1R em PDF agora, por 45 reais. Aos interessados, segue cópia em anexo.
Como eu suspeitava, é bem parecido!

webpage.description: The Technics SX-WSA1 was released in 1995 in a bold move by a company that had up until that point focused mostly on stereo equipment as well as organs and electric pianos. During this period, electronic synths were the domain of Yamaha, but Technics set out ot improve their synth over the competition in every way. Unfortunately, while they created a very competent synthesizer, Technics had no idea how to market and sell it. The high price tag for the time also meant less sales for them and, in the end, very few units of the SX-WSA1 were ever made.

text.text: The Famous Computer Cafe Has Now Been Archived Online

texts.text: You might think that TV stations or production houses would be great at archiving, but it’s not always the case. Particularly from the public access perspective. However, if you’re a fan of
you’re in luck! The beloved series

text.text: has now been preserved on The Internet Archive!

If you’re not familiar with the show, it was a radio program broadcast from 1983 to 1986. It was pumped out of a variety of radio stations in southern and central California in the period. The creators making sure to keep a copy of each episode in reel-to-reel tape format. For years, these tapes were tragically lost, until archivist [Kay Savetz] was able to recover some of them from a recent property sale. From there, a GoFundMe paid for digitization, and the show has been placed on The Internet Archive with the blessings of the original creators.

This is quite the cultural victory, particularly when you observe the list of guests on the show. Timothy Leary, Bill Gates, Jack Tramiel, and even Douglas Adams made appearances in the recovered recordings. Sadly, though, not all the tapes have been recovered. Episodes with Gene Roddenberry, Robert Moog, and Ray Bradbury are still lost to time.

texts.text: If you fancy a listen, 53 episodes presently exist

Take a trip back in time and hear from some technological visionaries—and futurists—speaking their minds at the very beginning of the microcomputer era! If you find any particularly salient gems, don’t hesitate to drop them

text.text: Everything You Wanted To Know About Early Macintosh Floppies

texts.text: Using a disk drive today is trivial. But back “in the day,” it was fairly complex both because the drives were simple and the CPUs were not powerful by today’s standards. [Thomas] has been working on a 68000 Mac emulator and found that low-level floppy information was scattered in different places. So he’s

text.text: gathered it all for us in one place

Low-level disk access has a lot of subtle details. For example, the Mac calibrates its speed control on boot. If your emulated drive just sets the correct speed and doesn’t respond to changes during calibration, the system will detect that as an error. Other details about spinning disks include the fact that inner tracks are shorter than outer track and may require denser recordings. Laying out sectors can also be tricky since you will lose performance if you, for example, read sector one and then miss sector two and have to wait for it to come back around. Disk sectors are often staggered for this reason.

Adding to the complexity is the controller — the IWM or Integrated Woz Machine — which has an odd scheme for memory mapping I/O. You should only access the odd bytes of the memory-mapped I/O. The details are all in the post.

texts.text: In a way, we don’t miss these days, but in other ways, we do. It wasn’t that long ago that
. Now it is a race to
on them while you still can.

Eu tenho uma placa de máquina caça-níquel chinesa chamada Amazonia King, da IGS. Muitos anos atrás eu fiz o dump das ROMs pro MAME. Mas... a CPU dessa placa, um ARM7, tem uma ROM de boot que fica escondida dentro da própria pastilha do processador.
E esse código de boot faz alguma inicialização do hardware e depois só executo o código do jogo, que fica numa ROM externa, se validar um checksum
sem essa ROM secreta, o jogo não roda
e se não passar na validação de checksum, aparece uma mensagem de erro, o que funciona como bloqueio contra execução de código modificado

mas teve um pessoal do MAME que desenvolveu um ataque trojan que consegue passar nessa validação, lê o conteúdo da ROM interna e gospe ela pra fora por meio de uma porta serial localizada em um pinio específico da PCB, onde eu preciso soldar um fiozinho pra ligar num conversor serial-USB (como um daqueles da FTDI, por exemplo)
me mandaram a ROM com o trojan pra eu fazer o dump
mas não me mandaram o código fonte
tentei desassemblar, mas a ROM é embaralhada
li o código fonte do driver no MAME e escrevi um script python pra desembaralhar e poder fazer o disasm

Dear Felipe Sanches,

I hope this email finds you well. I came across your name in the monthly update changelog of the MAME Project, along with your ongoing work on the Technics SX-KN5000 emulation project. Then  I found your contact information in the comments section of your YouTube channel. I am writing to inquire about the progress of this emulation project and to see if there are any opportunities for me to contribute.

As an electronic keyboard enthusiast from China, I, along with a few others, run a website called Electronic Keyboard Models & Demo Songs Database (https://demodb.org). Our website is dedicated to collecting information about electronic keyboard models, their specifications, and demo songs (primarily focusing on the demo songs). The goal is to preserve the culture and resources related to electronic keyboards. We currently have an emulator page that lists the electronic keyboards that can be run in MAME. We hope that in the future, the SX-KN5000 can also be featured on this page.

I understand that the implementation of this project requires a significant amount of effort. I was wondering if you have any estimate on when the project might be completed. Although Technics electronic keyboards are rarely seen in China, I am relatively familiar with electronic keyboards in general. I am wondering if there are any areas where I could offer my assistance. While I may not be able to contribute much in terms of coding (I can only write in js and python as an ametuer), I would be more than happy to help with artworks and documentation to the best of my abilities.
I look forward to hearing back from you!

Best regards,
DONG Guangyu
